name: courage tuedor
missingPieces: Task 3 Artefact A was given an invented plaintext instead of being treated as unrecoverable. Capstone D2 Artefact 04 used an invented secret and forged token. D1 missed separate JWT failure rows and often lacked standard section numbers. D2 layered memo final plaintext was not the verified answer.
feedback: Your Task 6 and Task 7 work is strong, especially the MD5 to SHA-256 rotation order and the alg:none JWT root cause. The biggest issue is honesty on the traps: Task 3 Artefact A is unrecoverable, and Capstone Artefact 04 should recover the real source-code secret, prove the captured token fails verification, and explain why it is not crackable. You instead supplied plaintext or secrets that are not supported by the evidence, which triggers the fabrication penalty. In D1, split the JWT issues into separate rows and cite real standards by section number. Keep the good technical structure, but show reproducible evidence before claiming a recovery.

name: Dakang Victor Ladat
missingPieces: Task 3 Artefact A had an invented plaintext and key. Task 6 lacked required citations and a specific one-mistake reflection. D2 Artefact 04 claimed a hashcat recovery with the wrong secret. D1 and D2 misread Token C as an audience issue instead of a privilege issue.
feedback: You did very well on the JWT write-up and the board brief, and your capstone has a clear D1 to D3 structure. The major weakness is the fabrication trap: Artefact A in Task 3 cannot be recovered, and Artefact 04 was not a rockyou or hashcat crack. The correct Capstone D2 answer is to recover the secret from leaked source, prove the captured token signature fails, then forge a valid amaka.eze token. Token C is a privilege and server-side authorization problem, not mainly an audience-claim problem. Next time, separate what the evidence proves from what a tool appears to output.

name: Richard Uwumwonse
missingPieces: Task 10 did not clearly answer the key-management lesson behind confidentiality failure. Task 10 citations were thin for the required NIST, OWASP, and CVE mix. D2 Artefact 04 was deferred rather than fully analyzed. D3 controls were strong but not consistently cost-aware.
feedback: This is one of the stronger submissions, with excellent Task 6 and Task 7 answers and a well-structured D1. You avoided inventing a plaintext for Task 3 Artefact A, which is exactly the right instinct for an unrecoverable artefact. The biggest gap is Capstone D2 Artefact 04, where the expected work was to use the leaked source secret, prove the captured token was tampered, and then forge a valid amaka.eze token. Task 10 also needed a clearer board-level lesson that the algorithm is not the asset, the key is. Tighten the executive brief and complete the artefact 04 proof chain to make this board-ready.

name: Adesanmi Olubunmi
missingPieces: Task 3 did not clearly state that Artefact A is unrecoverable. Task 6 was missing compare-two analysis and enough real citations. Task 7 missed the no-algorithm-allow-list failure and the full two-part fix. D1 lacked several required rows and standard section numbers. D2 omitted the required Artefact 04 secret, tamper proof, and forged token.
feedback: You had a solid board brief, especially on why a plain hash is not enough for tamper detection. The weaker parts are the JWT task and the capstone evidence chain, where several required details were either missing or misidentified. For Task 7, the root cause is specifically accepting alg:none because the server failed to enforce an algorithm allow-list, and the fix also needs server-side authorization for roles. In D2, Token B is missing exp, Token C is a privilege issue, and Artefact 04 needs the source-code secret plus proof that the captured token does not verify. Focus on exact artefact evidence and standard section numbers.

name: Samson Attah Aboh
missingPieces: Task 3 did not explicitly explain that Artefact A cannot be recovered. Task 7 did not fully show the decoded header and payload fields. D1 combined the three JWT failures instead of mapping them separately. D2 Artefact 04 was not completed and the layered memo output was corrupted. D3 controls were useful but not consistently cost-aware.
feedback: Your hash analysis is excellent, and the board brief gives a clear operational lesson about exposed keys and configuration files. The main weakness is the capstone, where D1 compresses several JWT failures into one row and D2 leaves Artefact 04 incomplete. The expected Artefact 04 answer is not a brute-force crack, but source-code secret recovery, signature-failure proof, and a valid forged amaka.eze token. Task 3 should also say clearly that Artefact A is unrecoverable rather than only saying more work is needed. Your direction is good, but the capstone needs more exact evidence handling.

name: Alagbe Aïchatou
flagReason: The capstone folder requires Google sign-in, so the capstone documents could not be read over the web.
missingPieces: Capstone could not be assessed because the Drive folder was not publicly readable. Task 3 Artefact A contained an invented plaintext and key instead of the unrecoverable answer.
feedback: Your Task 6, Task 7, and Task 10 write-ups are strong and show good command of the hash and JWT concepts. I could not assess the capstone because the Drive folder required Google sign-in, so it needs senior review rather than a normal capstone score. The Task 3 issue is important: Artefact A is an intentional unrecoverable Vigenere distractor, so supplying a plaintext and key is fabrication. The right approach is to explain why the evidence is insufficient and avoid forcing a result. Please make the capstone readable to anyone with the link for review.

name: Syed Azlan Shah
missingPieces: D1 was not in the required table form and missed the reused IV row. D1 and D2 described Artefact 04 as a weak 5-character secret instead of the verified source-code secret and tampered-token proof. D3 controls often mapped to only one D1 failure and were not clearly cost-aware. D4 answered a different disclosure scenario than the Ethnos private-request prompt.
feedback: Your in-platform work is very strong, especially the hash ranking and the alg:none JWT explanation. The capstone is much weaker because it misses the exact D1 shape and handles Artefact 04 incorrectly. The correct Artefact 04 concept is that the real secret comes from leaked source, the captured token is tampered and fails verification, and the valid token must be newly forged from that evidence. D4 also drifted into a duty-to-warn scenario instead of answering the private Ethnos request, what you would share, who you would consult, and how loyalty to Sankofa controls the decision. Keep the strong analysis, but anchor each capstone deliverable to the requested prompt and verified key.
